report:
**Conclusion: no—not based on reliable clinical evidence.** Ginkgo extract is widely marketed for tinnitus, but the best syntheses of randomized trials do not show a meaningful benefit over placebo for tinnitus when tinnitus is the main problem.

A Cochrane review of randomized controlled trials concluded that the limited evidence does **not** demonstrate ginkgo is effective for tinnitus as the primary complaint. Trials have varied in extract, dose, populations, and outcome measures; some small or lower-quality studies reported improvement, but this inconsistency does not establish a dependable treatment effect.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23543524/

This is consistent with an earlier systematic review of placebo-controlled trials, which was undertaken because individual trials had conflicting results.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/

Clinical guidance therefore advises against recommending ginkgo (or other dietary supplements) for **persistent, bothersome tinnitus**.  
https://www.entnet.org/quality-practice/quality-products/clinical-practice-guidelines/tinnitus/

This does not mean nobody will ever perceive improvement—tinnitus commonly fluctuates and placebo effects are substantial—but there is no good basis to expect ginkgo to reliably reduce loudness, distress, or functional impact. Also discuss ginkgo with a clinician or pharmacist before use, particularly if you take anticoagulant/antiplatelet medicines or have surgery planned, because supplements can have interactions and variable contents. Evidence-supported management is usually individualized and may include hearing assessment/hearing aids when indicated, tinnitus-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, and sound-based coping strategies.
